units.t: Physics Basics. Episode three.
In this episode: Magnetism: the invisible pull, Light and colour and How sound travels.
Part one. Magnetism: the invisible pull.
A fridge magnet, a compass needle and the southern lights are all showing you the same hidden force at work.
A rock that points north.
Long before anyone understood it, people noticed that certain dark rocks pulled iron towards them.
These lodestones are made of magnetite that has become naturally magnetised, possibly by lightning strikes.
In China, lodestone spoons were said to swing round to point in a fixed direction, and by the early twelfth century Chinese sailors steered with magnetised needles.
The compass later spread to the Arab world and Europe, where it helped make the great ocean voyages possible.
For centuries, nobody could say why a sliver of iron should care which way north was.
The answer lay deep inside atoms, and deep inside the Earth itself.
Tiny magnets lining up.
Each electron acts like a tiny bar magnet, thanks to a property called spin.
In most materials, including wood, plastic, water and your body, electrons pair up and their effects cancel.
In a few, unpaired electrons add together, and when enough point the same way, the object is magnetic.
Iron, nickel and cobalt are the classic magnetic metals.
Their atoms group into domains, each already magnetised.
In a nail the domains point every which way and cancel.
Bring a strong magnet near and they swing into line, so the nail becomes a magnet for a while.
Permanent magnets keep their domains aligned.
Heat scrambles the order.
Above the Curie point, about 770 degrees Celsius for iron, the magnetism disappears.
One force, many uses.
In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted saw a compass needle twitch when current flowed in a nearby wire: electricity can create magnetism.
In 1831 Michael Faraday showed the reverse.
Moving a magnet near a coil makes a current flow: electromagnetic induction.
In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell showed electricity and magnetism are one force, and predicted waves travelling at the speed of light.
Light, radio waves and X-rays are all electromagnetic waves.
Faraday's discovery powers your life.
Nearly every power station spins a magnet and a coil past each other so induction pushes current through the coil.
Motors run the trick backwards, in your fridge, washing machine and car windows.
MRI scanners line up hydrogen atoms in your body, then listen to their faint radio signals.
Earth's magnetic shield.
The Earth behaves like a huge magnet, which is why compasses work.
Its field is generated about 3,000 kilometres below your feet, in the outer core, where molten iron churns and flows like a natural dynamo.
The field reaches far into space and deflects most of the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun.
Some particles are funnelled towards the poles, where they hit gases in the upper atmosphere and make them glow.
In the Southern Hemisphere that glow is the aurora australis, sometimes seen from Tasmania.
The field is restless.
The magnetic poles wander, and every so often the whole field flips.
The last full reversal happened roughly 780,000 years ago.
Animals with a compass.
Humans need a compass, but many animals seem to carry one inside them.
Experiments show that migratory birds, sea turtles, salmon and even some insects use Earth's magnetic field to find their way.
Young loggerhead turtles appear to read the field's strength and angle to stay on course across thousands of kilometres of ocean.
How they sense it remains one of biology's lingering puzzles.
One leading idea is that light-sensitive proteins in birds' eyes react to magnetism, perhaps letting them 'see' the field as a faint pattern over their vision.
Another is that tiny grains of magnetite in some animals' bodies act like compass needles.
Both may be true in different species.
The key idea: People used magnetic rocks and compasses for thousands of years before anyone could explain why they work.
Part two. Light and colour.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe, it's both a wave and a particle, and colour doesn't exist without a brain to see it.
The cosmic speed limit.
Light moves at 299,792 kilometres per second in a vacuum, usually rounded to 300,000.
In one second it could circle the Earth about seven and a half times.
Moonlight takes about 1.
3 seconds to reach us, sunlight about 8 minutes and 20 seconds, and light from Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, over four years.
So when you look at distant stars, you're looking into the past: their light left years, centuries or millennia ago.
Light slows down in glass and water, but nothing with mass can ever reach its speed in a vacuum.
The hidden spectrum.
Light is electromagnetic radiation, a travelling wave of electric and magnetic fields, as Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell showed in the 1860s.
Visible light is only a narrow band, with wavelengths of about 400 to 700 nanometres.
Longer wavelengths include infrared, which you feel as heat, then microwaves and radio waves.
Shorter ones include ultraviolet, which causes sunburn, then X-rays and gamma rays.
They're all the same kind of thing, differing only in wavelength and energy.
Some animals sense beyond our range.
Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us, and some snakes detect the infrared glow of warm-blooded prey.
Bending light apart.
Smooth surfaces such as mirrors and still water reflect light at the same angle it arrives, which is why you see clear images in them.
When light passes from one material into another, such as air into water, it changes speed and bends.
This is refraction.
It makes a straw look broken in a glass and a pool look shallower than it is.
Lenses in glasses, cameras and eyes use it to focus light, and optical fibres use total internal reflection to carry internet data across oceans.
In the 1660s, Isaac Newton split sunlight with a prism, then recombined it, showing that white light is a mixture.
Violet bends most and red least.
Raindrops do the same job: light enters, reflects off the back and bends again on the way out.
You see a rainbow with the Sun behind you.
Why things have colour.
A banana looks yellow because it reflects mostly yellowish wavelengths and absorbs the rest.
A black T-shirt absorbs most light, so it heats up in the sun.
The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths far more than red, a process called Rayleigh scattering.
At sunrise and sunset light crosses far more air, so blue is scattered away and reds and oranges remain.
Clouds look white because their larger droplets scatter all colours equally.
Colour itself is made by your brain.
Your eyes have three types of cone cell, and the brain compares their signals.
That's why screens make almost any colour from red, green and blue dots, and why magenta, which matches no single wavelength, still looks real.
About 8 per cent of men and 0.
5 per cent of women of Northern European descent have some colour vision deficiency.
Wave, particle, laser.
In the early 1800s, Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw bands of light and dark, as overlapping water waves would make.
That was strong evidence for a wave.
But in 1905 Einstein explained the photoelectric effect, where light knocks electrons out of metal, by treating light as particles, later called photons.
He won the 1921 Nobel Prize for this, not for relativity.
Light acts as both, depending on how it's measured, a puzzle at the heart of quantum physics.
A laser produces waves of one wavelength, marching in step, in a narrow beam.
Einstein predicted the process in 1917 and Theodore Maiman built the first working laser in 1960.
Lasers now read barcodes, carry data, cut steel and reshape corneas.
Powerful pointers can damage eyes and are restricted in Australia.
The key idea: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second, and nothing with mass can match that speed.
Part three. How sound travels.
Every voice, song and thunderclap is just air being squeezed and stretched, and the physics explains everything from echoes to sonic booms.
A wave you can't see.
Clap your hands and you shove the air between them outwards.
Those molecules bump their neighbours, which bump theirs, and a ripple of squashed and stretched air spreads in every direction.
That ripple is sound.
It is a pressure wave, and the air itself barely moves: each molecule nudges back and forth and passes the push along, like a ripple running down a slinky.
When the wave reaches you, it pushes and pulls on your eardrum, which vibrates in step.
Tiny bones in your middle ear pass the vibration to the fluid-filled cochlea, where thousands of hair cells turn it into nerve signals.
Your brain turns those signals into a friend's laugh or a favourite song.
The speed of sound.
In air at about 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels about 343 metres every second, roughly a kilometre in three seconds.
Light is nearly a million times faster, which is why you see a batter hit the ball across a cricket ground, or a distant firework burst, a moment before you hear it.
Sound is faster in warm air than cold, and much faster through liquids and solids, where closely packed particles pass the push along.
In seawater it travels at roughly 1,500 metres per second, and in steel several times faster again.
That is why you can hear an approaching train through the rails before you hear it through the air.
Pitch and loudness.
Pitch depends on frequency, the number of waves passing each second, measured in hertz.
The A above middle C, used to tune orchestras, is 440 hertz.
Young people typically hear about 20 to 20,000 hertz, shrinking with age.
Elephants use infrasound below our range, while dogs, bats and dolphins hear ultrasound above it.
Overtones make instruments sound different on the same note.
Loudness is measured in decibels on a logarithmic scale: every 10 decibels means ten times more sound energy, which we hear as roughly twice as loud.
A library is around 30 to 40, conversation around 60 and a loud concert well over 100.
Long or repeated exposure above roughly 85 decibels can permanently damage the hair cells in your inner ear.
Healthdirect can help with ringing or muffled hearing.
Echoes and the Doppler effect.
Shout across a valley and the sound bounces back as an echo.
Many bats send out rapid, high-pitched calls and judge the distance, size and texture of insects from the echoes, in total darkness.
This is echolocation.
Ships use sonar to map the seafloor, and medical ultrasound builds an image from echoes off organs, which is how many parents first see their baby.
An ambulance siren drops in pitch as it passes, though the siren has not changed.
As it approaches, waves bunch up and arrive more often; as it leaves, they stretch out.
This is the Doppler effect, described by Christian Doppler in 1842.
It works for all waves: police radar measures car speed, weather radar tracks wind in storms, and astronomers measure how fast galaxies move away.
Silence and sonic booms.
Films are full of roaring explosions in space, but real space is silent.
Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, and the near vacuum between planets has almost none to carry it.
Astronauts on a spacewalk talk by radio, which uses electromagnetic waves that need no medium.
Back on Earth, something interesting happens when an object travels faster than sound.
A supersonic jet outruns its own pressure waves, which pile up into a cone-shaped shock wave.
When it sweeps over you, you hear a sudden sonic boom.
The first officially confirmed supersonic flight was made by American pilot Chuck Yeager in the Bell X-1 rocket plane in 1947.
A cracking whip makes a tiny sonic boom too.
The key idea: Sound is a travelling ripple of pressure, not a stream of air rushing from the source to your ear.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What stands out about the early history of magnets?
Answer. People used them long before knowing why.
Question two. What does it mean to look at a distant star?
Answer. You see light that left it centuries ago or more.
Question three. What actually travels from a sound source to your ear?
Answer. A ripple of pressure in the air.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
